**Verdict: ILLEGAL.** This does not work as constructed. He has $79,300,000 left over 2 years, which stretches over 5 seasons at $15,860,000 a year in dead money. We are already carrying $9,300,000 in stretched money from earlier waivers, and the two stack. The ceiling is $21,088,200 -- fifteen percent of the cap in any one season. ground_truth.reason: the stretch is not legal as structured: $25,160,000 of dead money would exceed the $21,088,200 ceiling by $4,071,800 per season. The player would have to give back roughly $20,359,000 for the waiver to work

Ownership wants us out of the second apron. Walk me through how we do it.

We are $5,213,223 over the second apron, at $226,899,223 against a line of $221,686,000. Start with what is closed to us. Over the second apron we cannot combine two salaries into one trade, and we cannot send cash. That rules out most of the constructions that would normally solve this, and it means every solution is a single salary going out. Salaries large enough to clear the gap on their own: Tobias Dumont at $5,495,050 clears it with $281,827 to spare. Luka Ellington at $6,305,096 clears it with $1,091,873 to spare. Kristaps Duval at $6,400,111 clears it with $1,186,888 to spare. Dante Halvorsen at $6,584,596 clears it with $1,371,373 to spare. Any of those gets us under, assuming nothing comes back. That assumption is the hard part -- we need a partner with room to absorb the salary outright, and they will want something for the favor. Draft compensation is the usual price. The alternative is finishing the season here and accepting the pick freeze. That is a real option if the roster is good enough, and a bad one if it is not.

Which exceptions does a team over the first apron lose, and which does it keep?

What can a second-apron team still do in a trade?

Here is the list, and it is a short one. Over the second apron ($207,824,000 in 2025-26) a team can still trade one salary for another at 100% matching, sign minimum contracts, and re-sign its own free agents using Bird rights. That is genuinely all. What it cannot do: aggregate two salaries into one trade, send cash in any trade, use any mid-level exception including the taxpayer version, acquire anyone by sign-and-trade, or sign a mid-season waivee who was earning above the non-taxpayer mid-level. If you tell me where a specific team sits, I can say which of these actually bind.

Which exceptions does a team over the first apron lose, and which does it keep?

Which moves trigger a hard cap, and at which level?

Here is the list, and it is a short one. Six moves hard-cap a team at the first apron: using the non-taxpayer mid-level, using the bi-annual exception, acquiring a player by sign-and-trade, taking back more than 100% of outgoing salary, using a prior-year traded player exception, and signing a mid-season waivee who was earning above the non-taxpayer mid-level. Four hard-cap a team at the second apron: using the taxpayer mid-level, aggregating salaries in a trade, sending cash in a trade, and using an outgoing sign-and-traded player's salary for matching. The room exception triggers no hard cap at all. Whichever applies runs through June 30 and is never retroactive. If you tell me where a specific team sits, I can say which of these actually bind.

Which exceptions does a team over the first apron lose, and which does it keep?

Straightforward enough to answer in full. Over the first apron ($195,945,000 in 2025-26) a team loses four things: the full non-taxpayer mid-level, the bi-annual exception, the ability to acquire a player by sign-and-trade, and access to the buyout market for anyone whose pre-waiver salary exceeded the non-taxpayer mid-level. It is also capped at taking back 100% of outgoing salary in a trade, and it cannot use a traded player exception generated in a prior league year. We need to get under the second apron before the deadline. What are our options, and what are we giving up?

We are $9,949,569 over the second apron, at $198,880,569 against a line of $188,931,000. Start with what is closed to us. Over the second apron we cannot combine two salaries into one trade, and we cannot send cash. That rules out most of the constructions that would normally solve this, and it means every solution is a single salary going out. Salaries large enough to clear the gap on their own: Isaiah Nakamura at $12,655,373 clears it with $2,705,804 to spare. Devonte Marsh at $14,393,105 clears it with $4,443,536 to spare. Kobe Halvorsen at $25,722,925 clears it with $15,773,356 to spare. Trey Cordero at $41,687,696 clears it with $31,738,127 to spare. Any of those gets us under, assuming nothing comes back. That assumption is the hard part -- we need a partner with room to absorb the salary outright, and they will want something for the favor. Draft compensation is the usual price. The alternative is finishing the season here and accepting the pick freeze. That is a real option if the roster is good enough, and a bad one if it is not.
